source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree
finding: Adversaries from the RPD and heuristics-and-biases camps agree on when to trust intuition. Skilled intuition needs a high-validity environment with learnable cues, and enough practice with feedback.
numbers: Two conditions: (1) environment with valid cues, (2) adequate opportunity to learn them. Chess masters need about 10,000 hours (Chase and Simon).
quote: Skilled intuitions will only develop in an environment that provides valid cues to the situation.
limits: Authors are the two rivals, so this is a negotiated view, not a test. No new data.
agent_relevance: Keep-first mode is only safe where the task has stable cues and the agent has seen many similar cases. Gate it on task type, not on the agent's feeling of certainty.

source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree (RPD description)
finding: Their description of the founding study: commanders mostly generated a single option, evaluated it by mental simulation, modified it, and moved to the next option only if needed.
numbers: Initial hypothesis was that commanders compare a pair of options. This was wrong; usually one option was generated.
quote: In fact, the commanders usually generated only a single option, and that was all they needed.
limits: Secondhand account of Klein, Calderwood and Clinton-Cirocco (1986); the original report was not readable this session (DTIC blocked).
agent_relevance: This is the exact generate-test loop: one candidate, simulate, repair, then next candidate. Easy to implement as a scaffold step.

source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree (confidence)
finding: Subjective confidence is a poor sign that an intuition is valid. No inner marker separates a skilled intuition from one made by a weak heuristic.
numbers: Confidence is driven by coherence and ease of the story, not by validity (Einhorn and Hogarth 1978 cited).
quote: There is no subjective marker that distinguishes correct intuitions from intuitions that are produced by highly imperfect heuristics.
limits: A claim from the review; the supporting studies were not individually opened.
agent_relevance: A keep-first agent must not use its own stated confidence as the gate to skip checking. Use external cues (task familiarity, past hit rate) instead.

source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree (fractionated expertise)
finding: Experts are skilled on some tasks and not others, even within one profession (nurses, physicians, auditors appear on both Shanteau's good and bad lists).
numbers: Shanteau (1992): good performance for livestock judges, weather, chess, pilots; poor for stockbrokers, clinical psychologists, admissions officers, intelligence analysts.
limits: Shanteau list is a review of mixed older studies; task features given are predictability, experience, feedback, static stimuli.
agent_relevance: Recognition-style expertise cannot be assumed to transfer across sub-tasks. Route per task, not per agent.

source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree (algorithms vs clinical judgment)
finding: Statistical rules beat or tied expert clinical judgment in nearly all studies reviewed. This is the main limit on recognition-based decisions in low-validity domains.
numbers: Algorithms better in about half the studies (n=63), no difference in n=65, clinicians better in only n=8 (counts read from text with garbled symbols).
limits: Counts read from a garbled PDF layout. Mostly clinical psychology and medicine.
agent_relevance: When a simple scored rule exists for the task, the scaffold should prefer it over recognition.

source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree (Goldberg bootstrapping)
finding: Models of individual judges predicted better than the judges themselves, showing that inconsistency hurts expert accuracy.
numbers: Goldberg (1970): 29 clinicians, MMPI profiles of 861 patients, 11 scales; bootstrap models almost always more accurate than the judges.
limits: Old study, one task (psychotic vs neurotic).
agent_relevance: Recognition output varies run to run. Sample several first-options and vote, or fix the cue weights.

source: Fan, Sun, McNeese, Yen (2005) Extending the RPD model to support human-agent collaboration (R-CAST)
finding: An RPD-based software agent (R-CAST) with expectancy monitoring let human-agent teams hold up under time pressure much better than all-human teams in a command simulation.
numbers: 6 human teams vs 6 human-agent teams, each run on 9 scenarios of 48 joint-tasks. Enemy destroyed: human-agent significantly better, p<0.001 (S3 role); supply delivery p=0.211 (not significant). At maximum speed human teams were near failure while human-agent teams destroyed 36% of enemy units.
limits: Graduate student participants, a single simulated task (DDD), small teams, no human expert control. The agent was hand-built with cases elicited from testing runs.
agent_relevance: Shows RPD-as-architecture works when the case library is built from the task. Monitoring of expectancies (drop the plan when the world differs) is a cheap addition to keep-first.

source: Fan et al. (2005) R-CAST (adaptation)
finding: When the human told the agent the attack pattern had changed, the agent dropped the current course of action and chose another, based on expectancy monitoring.
numbers: Scenarios of 48 joint-tasks with 6 moving patterns; adaptation worked for all pattern changes where the human reported the change in time.
limits: Demonstrated by example cases, not a measured rate. Depends on the human reporting the change.
agent_relevance: Keep-first needs a break rule: write down what you expect to see after acting, and revert when it fails.

source: Kopka & Feufel (2026) Increasing LLM accuracy for care-seeking advice using prompts reflecting human reasoning strategies (JMIR Biomed Eng)
finding: A prompt telling the model to use RPD (match to typical case, simulate the usual decision, modify if it fails) raised triage accuracy a little over a plain prompt.
numbers: 10 ChatGPT models, 45 vignettes, 10 runs each, 3 prompts = 13,500 assessments. Accuracy: default 63.3% (CI 61.9-64.7), RPD prompt 67.6% (66.3-69), data-frame prompt 66.7% (65.3-68). Odds ratio RPD vs default 2.26 (z=8.69, P<.001).
limits: Single domain (care-seeking triage). Only 2 emergency cases, so no safety conclusion. Only OpenAI/ChatGPT models. A preprint version reported 70.2% vs 64.7%, so numbers moved between versions. No ablation of which part of the RPD prompt helped.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM test of the RPD scaffold. Effect is real but modest (+4.3 points). Cheap to include as a prompt step.

source: Kopka & Feufel (2026) Increasing LLM accuracy for care-seeking advice using prompts reflecting human reasoning strategies (JMIR Biomed Eng) (reasoning vs non-reasoning)
finding: The RPD prompt helped reasoning models more than non-reasoning models, but the newest models gained nothing or lost.
numbers: Interaction OR 2.15 (z=4.05, P<.001) for the RPD prompt. GPT-5.2 Instant: default 57.8%, RPD 56.4%, data-frame 55.3%. GPT-5.2 Thinking: 52.0% vs 53.1% vs 51.8%. GPT-4.1: 64.4% default vs 72.7% RPD.
limits: Per-model CIs about plus or minus 4-5 points, so the GPT-5.2 differences are within noise. The newest models scored lower than older ones under every prompt.
agent_relevance: Gains from reasoning-style prompts can shrink on stronger models. Test the scaffold step against the current base model before keeping it.

source: Kopka & Feufel (2026) Increasing LLM accuracy for care-seeking advice using prompts reflecting human reasoning strategies (JMIR Biomed Eng) (per case and per class)
finding: The RPD prompt moved models toward self-care advice, correcting over-caution, but it also hurt some cases.
numbers: Self-care accuracy 13.4% default to 29.8% RPD (24.6% data-frame). RPD prompt raised accuracy on 18 of 45 cases (40%, median +18%) and lowered it on 13 (29%, median -5%); 12 of 13 decreases were nonemergency cases. Emergency: 100% default, 98% RPD. GPT-4.1 self-care 0% default to 43.8% RPD.
limits: Two emergency vignettes only. Self-care base accuracy was very low, so some of the gain is a shift in answer bias.
agent_relevance: Part of the gain is a shift in the answer prior, not better reasoning. Check calibration, not just accuracy.

source: Kopka & Feufel (2026) Increasing LLM accuracy for care-seeking advice using prompts reflecting human reasoning strategies (JMIR Biomed Eng) (consistency)
finding: The RPD prompt made answers a bit less repeatable across runs but raised the chance that the correct answer appeared at least once.
numbers: Fleiss kappa median 0.766 default, 0.717 RPD, 0.751 data-frame. Correct at least once in 10 trials: 73.1% default vs 82.2% RPD vs 78.4% data-frame. Same most-frequent answer 76.9% default vs 66.9% RPD.
limits: Difference in modal-answer consistency was not significant (z=1.50, P=.13 for RPD).
agent_relevance: Supports sample-then-verify: RPD diversifies candidates, so a checker step is needed to pick among them.

source: Reale, Salwei, Militello et al. (2023) Decision-making during high-risk events: a systematic literature review (J Cogn Eng Decis Mak)
finding: A review of 32 studies of professionals in crises found RPD strategies in every study that looked, but analytic strategies were also common, mostly where time pressure was lower or multiple explanations were trained.
numbers: 32 studies, 19 in healthcare; RPD reported in all studies that analysed strategy; three surgeon studies found RPD used about half the time (Pauley 2011, 2013).
limits: Qualitative synthesis, no effect size on decision quality. Mostly interview or self-report. Some studies could not separate RPD from rule-following (oil installation, Kaempf 1996).
agent_relevance: Both modes exist in practice. The scaffold should switch: recognition under time pressure, comparison when time allows or the case is unfamiliar.

source: Reale et al. (2023) (naval officers)
finding: In the Kaempf et al. (1996) study of naval tactical officers, most recognition-generated actions were run without further evaluation, and the main work was situation assessment.
numbers: 78% of recognition-generated actions implemented without further evaluation (Kaempf et al. 1996, as reported).
limits: Secondhand figure. Standard operating procedure and rules of engagement may drive the pattern, not expertise.
agent_relevance: In a military setting the hard step is diagnosing the situation, not comparing options. Put the effort in the assessment states.

source: Reale et al. (2023) (phases)
finding: Eleven studies found RPD phases are not strictly sequential: they can be skipped, overlap, or reorder as events unfold.
numbers: 11 studies explored RPD aspects (Cohen-Hatton 2015, Cristancho 2013 and others).
limits: Observational; surgeons add a pre-operative plan which changes the model (three-stage cycle with a reconciliation step).
agent_relevance: Do not hard-code a linear pipeline. Allow re-diagnosis mid-simulation.

source: Understanding a player's decision-making process in team sports: systematic review (Sports 2021)
finding: Sport studies support a split of intuition vs option generation, and time available decides which wins.
numbers: Basevitch et al.: experts beat near-experts; intuitive first responses were more effective when time was short, generating more options was better when more time was available. Klatt et al.: Brazilian players beat German players on both first-option accuracy and number of options. Musculus: only less-is-more supported.
limits: Video-based tasks, small samples, judged against expert coach rankings; authors criticise decontextualised tasks.
agent_relevance: Time budget is the key moderator: keep-first when short, widen the option list when long.

source: Raab & Gigerenzer (2015) The power of simplicity: fast-and-frugal heuristics in performance science (Front Psychol)
finding: Take-the-first (Johnson & Raab 2003) is a formal version of keep-first: search options in order of validity, stop after two to three, choose the first. It predicts that more options means worse choices, unlike long-term working memory models.
numbers: Evidence in handball (Johnson & Raab 2003) and basketball (Hepler & Feltz). Spread to nursing, navigation, law, medicine. Influenced by situation, emotion, personality.
limits: Review by the heuristic's own proponents. Option validity is assumed learned from feedback, so novices should not show it.
agent_relevance: A rival model (more options, better choice) makes a clear prediction; test which holds for the agent's candidates.

source: Hepler & Feltz (2012) Take the first heuristic, self-efficacy, and decision-making in sport (J Exp Psychol Appl)
finding: A conceptual replication with students on video basketball tasks supported take-the-first, but not the claims about consistency or confidence.
numbers: N=72, 13 trials in each of two tasks. Heuristic used on 70% of trials; earlier options were better than later ones. No difference in dynamic inconsistency or confidence by number of options. Higher self-efficacy meant more take-the-first and fewer options.
limits: Abstract only was read. Students, not experts; video task. Self-efficacy link is correlational.
agent_relevance: Earlier-better holds even in non-experts here, which is evidence for first-candidate quality, though weaker than for experts.

source: Raab & Johnson (2007) Expertise-based differences in search and option-generation strategies (J Exp Psychol Appl)
finding: Experts, near-experts and non-experts generated the same number of options on average but differed in the quality of first and final choices. Eye tracking verified the strategies inferred from verbal protocols.
numbers: 2-year longitudinal study of handball athletes; option count equal across expertise groups; quality of initial and final choices differed by expertise.
limits: Abstract only was read; no effect sizes available to me.
agent_relevance: Expert advantage lies in the quality of the first candidate, not in search effort. Ground the first candidate in retrieval of similar cases.

source: Raab & Laborde (2011) When to blink and when to think (Res Q Exerc Sport)
finding: Handball players with an intuitive preference chose faster and better in attack situations, and experts were more intuitive than near-experts and non-experts.
numbers: 54 male and female players of different expertise levels, lab-based choices.
limits: Abstract only. Lab tasks; preference is self-reported; confounded with expertise.
agent_relevance: Intuitive style is tied to expertise, not a free speedup for novices.

source: Flin et al. (2007) How do surgeons make intraoperative decisions? (Qual Saf Health Care)
finding: Surgeons are proposed to use four strategies: intuitive (recognition-primed), rule-based, option comparison, and creative. Very few studies had directly examined them.
numbers: Four strategies; evidence base described as scant.
limits: Conceptual review, no counts. Abstract only.
agent_relevance: The four-way split (recognise, rule, compare, create) matches a router design for the scaffold.

source: Yu (2016) Stress potentiates decision biases: SIDI model (Neurobiol Stress)
finding: Stress shifts people from deliberation to intuition, which strengthens decision biases. This is a boundary condition on keep-first: stress pushes people into that mode whether or not it fits.
numbers: Review of stress studies; mixed effects on risk taking (stress reduced the framing effect in one dice-task study, Pabst 2013b).
limits: Review of lab stress studies, mostly students, not experts under real stress. Read in part.
agent_relevance: Tight limits on a model can push it into first-answer mode. Do not let budget pressure silently disable checking.

source: Police training review (Front Psychol 2019) Complex motor learning and police training
finding: Intuitive decisions are fast and habitual and hard to modify, so training must cement correct patterns before relying on them. RPD is described as situation awareness plus mental simulation.
numbers: No numeric result read.
limits: Perspective article; read only the RPD passage.
agent_relevance: Wrong patterns learned early are sticky; seed any case library only with verified cases.

source: Naturalistic decision-making in sport: advances into the RPD model (Front Psychol 2022)
finding: Review says the empirical evidence for a continuum from intuitive to analytical decisions in sport is inconsistent, and that expert athletes picked their first option in about 80% of decisions.
numbers: About 80% first-option choice cited from earlier sport research; lack of consistent evidence for the intuitive-analytical continuum.
limits: Secondary citation of the 80% figure; no source or N was given in the text I read.
agent_relevance: The 80% figure repeats across domains but has no clear primary source here; do not quote it as a measured rate.

source: Fire Engineering (trade article) Fireground command decisions
finding: A trade piece quotes Klein: fireground commanders make 80% of decisions in under a minute (Sources of Power p.4). It gives no sample size or method.
numbers: 80% of decisions in under 1 minute. A web search snippet (not the page I opened) attributed to Klein et al. that under 12% of critical decision points showed comparison of alternatives.
limits: Secondhand, not from the primary report. The 12% figure comes from a search snippet, so unverified.
agent_relevance: Use as a pointer only. Primary numbers must come from Klein, Calderwood and Clinton-Cirocco (1986) or Klein (1998).

source: Wikipedia, Recognition primed decision
finding: The page gives no studies or numbers. It names the limit: RPD needs extensive experience and fails when situations are unusual or misidentified.
numbers: No figures. Page is marked as needing more citations.
limits: Thin source; shows the public summary of RPD has no quantitative support attached.
agent_relevance: The known failure is mis-recognition: a confident wrong match. The scaffold needs a cue-mismatch check.

source: Klein, Calderwood, Clinton-Cirocco (1986) Rapid decision making on the fire ground (TR 796)
finding: Founding study: interviews with experienced fireground commanders. Commanders rarely compared options; a recognition-primed model was synthesised from the accounts.
numbers: 26 commanders, mean 23 years experience (from a web search summary); other counts not verified.
limits: Not opened: DTIC returned a block page. Retrospective interviews with no outcome measure; coding by the authors; no control group; no test of whether the first option beat other options.
agent_relevance: Core weakness for our purposes: no proof that keep-first beats compare. Evidence on first-option quality comes from the sport studies instead.

source: Klein, Wolf, Militello, Zsambok (1995) Characteristics of skilled option generation in chess (OBHDP)
finding: Cited by Kahneman and Klein (2009) as a lab test of RPD. Details not read.
numbers: Not verified this session.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Candidate evidence that the first generated option is the best one for experts; needs checking.

source: Johnson & Raab (2003) Take the first: option-generation and resulting choices (OBHDP)
finding: Origin of the take-the-first model in handball. Raab & Gigerenzer 2015 describe it as search of options in order of validity, stopping after two to three.
numbers: Exact N and effect sizes not verified.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Replication by Hepler and Feltz (N=72) was read via abstract.
